A Sanger chromatogram is the primary evidence trace of capillary sequencing: four fluorescent channels are recorded as a function of elution time, and the base caller assigns one nucleotide per peak. The figure is still the standard way to inspect heterozygous sites, indel boundaries, and low-quality tails before a variant is accepted. This tutorial rebuilds the publication layout from raw trace-like data: four colour-coded channels, called bases, and a quality track aligned on the same x axis.

## Setup

-   System Requirements: Cross-platform (Linux/MacOS/Windows)

-   Programming language: R

-   Dependent packages: `ggplot2`; `dplyr`; `tidyr`; `patchwork`; `scales`

```{r packages setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, output=FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("ggplot2")
if (!requireNamespace("dplyr", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("dplyr")
if (!requireNamespace("tidyr", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("tidyr")
if (!requireNamespace("patchwork", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("patchwork")
if (!requireNamespace("scales", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("scales")

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(patchwork)
library(scales)
```

```{r}
sessioninfo::session_info("attached")
```

## Data Preparation

The input produced by an `.ab1` reader is a matrix of fluorescence intensities (`scan` rows by four dye columns) plus a called sequence and per-base quality scores. We simulate 96 bases with Gaussian peaks, local baseline noise, one heterozygous C/T position, and a low-quality tail. The simulation is intentionally transparent: every visual feature in the figure maps to a column that a real trace reader would provide.

```{r load data, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(4351)

bases <- c("A", "C", "G", "T")
dye_colours <- c(A = "#2E8B57", C = "#2166AC", G = "#222222", T = "#C51B1F")
n_base <- 96

called <- sample(bases, n_base, replace = TRUE, prob = c(.3, .2, .22, .28))
called[61] <- "Y"                       # C/T heterozygote
called[88:96] <- sample(bases, 9, replace = TRUE)

position <- seq_len(n_base)
base_amp <- rnorm(n_base, 860, 55)
base_amp[61] <- 900
scan <- seq(1, n_base, length.out = n_base * 24)
peak <- function(centre, sigma = 0.30) {
  dnorm(scan, centre, sigma) / dnorm(centre, centre, sigma)
}

## Each channel carries a peak only where that base was called. The C/T site
## receives two half-height peaks, which is the evidence a heterozygote call needs.
make_channel <- function(ch) {
  y <- numeric(length(scan))
  for (i in seq_along(called)) {
    if (called[i] == ch) y <- y + base_amp[i] * peak(i)
    if (called[i] == "Y" && ch %in% c("C", "T")) {
      y <- y + 0.58 * base_amp[i] * peak(i)
    }
  }
  y
}

trace <- tibble(scan = scan) |>
  mutate(A = make_channel("A"), C = make_channel("C"),
         G = make_channel("G"), T = make_channel("T")) |>
  pivot_longer(-scan, names_to = "channel", values_to = "signal") |>
  mutate(
    base_index = scan,
    taper = ifelse(base_index >= 84, pmax(0.38, 1 - (base_index - 83) / 22), 1),
    signal = pmax(0, signal * taper + 24 + rnorm(n(), 0, 12))
  )

quality <- tibble(
  base_index = position,
  quality = pmin(60, pmax(9, round(rnorm(n_base, 37, 8)))),
  called = called
) |>
  mutate(quality = ifelse(base_index >= 84, quality - 18, quality),
         quality = pmax(5, quality))

head(trace)
```

## Visualization

### 1. Four-Channel Trace with Called Bases

The classic view overlays the four dye channels on a common time axis and prints the called base above the trace. Colour is reserved for the channel; the called sequence stays black so it remains readable in print.

```{r}
#| label: fig-1.1FourChannelTrace
#| fig-cap: "Sanger trace: four fluorescent channels, called bases, and the C/T heterozygote at position 61."
#| out.width: "100%"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-dpi: 300

base_labels <- quality |>
  mutate(y = 1120, label = called)

p_trace <- ggplot(trace, aes(scan, signal, colour = channel)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.55, alpha = 0.95) +
  geom_text(data = base_labels, aes(base_index, y, label = label),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3.1, family = "mono") +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 60.35, xmax = 61.65, ymin = -130, ymax = 1180,
           fill = "#F4A582", alpha = 0.12, colour = NA) +
  annotate("text", x = 61, y = 1240, label = "C/T heterozygote",
           size = 3.1, colour = "#8C2D04") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = dye_colours, name = "Dye channel") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 25, 50, 75, 96),
                     expand = c(0.005, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.06))) +
  labs(x = "Base position", y = "Fluorescence intensity (RFU)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.key.width = unit(8, "mm"),
    axis.line = element_line(linewidth = 0.35),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(colour = "#EBEBEB", linewidth = 0.25)
  )

p_quality <- ggplot(quality, aes(base_index, quality, fill = quality < 20)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.78) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 20, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.35,
             colour = "#7F7F7F") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#4D4D4D", `TRUE` = "#D6604D"),
                    guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0.005, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Phred Q") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    axis.line = element_line(linewidth = 0.35)
  )

p_trace / p_quality + plot_layout(heights = c(4.4, 1.2))
```

### 2. Heterozygous Peak Decomposition

A heterozygous call is not a cosmetic annotation: two channels must rise at the same position with roughly half the amplitude of a homozygous peak. Plotting the local window makes the evidence auditable and separates a true variant from a dye blob or a neighbouring-base shoulder.

```{r}
#| label: fig-1.2Heterozygote
#| fig-cap: "Local decomposition of the C/T site: overlapping C and T peaks at half height, with the surrounding homozygous peaks for scale."
#| out.width: "78%"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-dpi: 300

local <- trace |>
  filter(scan > 56.4, scan < 65.6) |>
  mutate(channel = factor(channel, levels = bases))

local_labels <- quality |>
  filter(base_index %in% 57:65) |>
  mutate(y = 1080)

ggplot(local, aes(base_index, signal, colour = channel)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = local |> filter(base_index == 61,
                                    channel %in% c("C", "T")),
             size = 2.1, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(data = local_labels, aes(base_index, y, label = called),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3.4, family = "mono") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = dye_colours, name = "Dye channel") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 57:65, expand = c(0.03, 0.03)) +
  labs(
    x = "Base position",
    y = "Fluorescence intensity (RFU)",
    title = "C/T heterozygote at position 61",
    subtitle = "Both channels peak together at about 58% of a homozygous signal"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "right",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "#555555", size = 9.5)
  )
```

::: callout-tip
**Practice tips**

-   Read the trace in the **called-base frame**, not the raw scan index: mobility shifts differ between dyes, so `.ab1` readers align channels before plotting.
-   A heterozygous site needs two channels at the same position with comparable height. A shoulder from the neighbouring base is usually asymmetric and narrower.
-   Keep the quality track directly below the trace with a shared x scale. A low-quality tail is then visible as a visual break rather than an unexplained gap in the sequence.
-   For publication, export vector traces when the source tool allows it; 300 dpi PNG is the minimum for raster panels.
:::

## Application

Sanger traces remain the confirmation layer for CRISPR edits, plasmid constructs, and clinical variants. The same four-channel layout generalises to any capillary electrophoresis signal (SSR genotyping, methylation-sensitive Sanger, and bisulfite sequencing). In a multi-read assembly view, the per-base quality track becomes the consensus model that decides which discrepant positions are real.
